TASK: READ AND ANSWER

Below is a two-page executive summary. Read it, and answer the questions using only what it says. Do not use anything you know from elsewhere.

1. Can each of these be said from page 1 alone? (a) SI readiness is complex, fast-moving and beyond any one expert, and we use SI to solve it; (b) we built a decision support system that measures a site's real state, maps it to a standard framework, and says what to fix first for the best value; (c) anyone from an executive to a site administrator can ask it questions and get cited explanations at their own level; (d) we ran the public tier on all 16 federal statistical agencies and found standout results. Answer yes or no for each, and name any that cannot.
2. What on page 1 would a chief information officer new to the term SI not understand? List each such thing.
3. What is said twice? Name each point made more than once.
4. What detail could be cut without loss? Name each.
5. Name every term on either page, page 1 or the grid on page 2, that a chief information officer new to the term SI would not already know. List each such term, or say none.

Return ONLY a JSON object, with no prose before or after it and no code fence:
{"q1": "...", "q2": "...", "q3": "...", "q4": "...", "q5": "..."}

SUMMARY
Prepared 15 October 2026.

SI readiness is how well an SI system, one that finds, reads and uses data on its own, can reach an agency's data, understand it, and use it correctly. People increasingly reach official statistics through such systems, so when those systems cannot find or understand federal data, the public is left with stale or second-hand numbers. SI readiness runs across data publishing, web practice, metadata standards and policy at once and moves fast, so no one person holds all of it, and we meet an SI problem with SI.

## What we built

This is a decision support system, not a site checker: it measures what a machine actually meets on an agency's site, rather than what the agency says about itself. It maps each result onto a readiness framework, built on the four qualities USAFacts set out (that data be accessible, understandable, accurate and open) with three more added, and puts every result on one standard scale so agencies can be set side by side. It then says what to fix first for the best value, the cheap high-value fixes before the larger ones, where how much a fix is worth is a rated judgment under a stated rubric, not a measurement.

## Who can use it, and why its advice can be trusted

An executive, a site administrator, a data producer or anyone working in the data's life can ask it questions and get answers at their own level, so no one need be expert in every field it touches. The advice rests on a knowledge graph of the research, standards and policy, which the system reads to give answers with their sources attached. When newer evidence replaces a source, the graph keeps the old one as history but stops it shaping advice.

## Measured in three tiers, by who can run them

The checks fall into three tiers by who can run them: a public tier anyone can run with free, open tools; an agency-enabled tier that needs an agency to turn something on; and a paid-tool tier. The public tier matters most, because it is what any such system, and any member of the public, meets, not only the largest commercial crawlers. The grid on the next page is the public tier, agency by agency.

## What we found

This measurement covers all 16 federal statistical agencies. A plain, identified machine client is frequently refused before it can read anything, and much of what it looks for is not served at all. Resources that agencies do publish often cannot be reached by a machine that starts at the data page.

## One caution

Any single score can be gamed, so we design around what the public can actually reach: readiness is judged where real users and their tools meet the data.

The fix under each check:

- Data offered in a machine format: Link a data file from the product page and serve it with its own media type.
- A documented machine interface: Expose the product through a machine interface and publish its description.
- A full dataset download: Link a bulk download of the product from the product page.
- Crawlers allowed to reach the data: Serve a robots.txt that permits the data paths for the crawlers you want to allow.
- The data is listed for discovery: List the product address in the discovery file that is already served.
- Structured markup describes the data: Type the product page's existing markup as a dataset.
- A machine readable release date: Publish a release date for the product.
- A machine first entry point: Publish a machine-first entry point for the product.
- Data tools answer a machine: Return a real status for routes that do not exist.
- Methodology in reachable structured text: Link the methodology from the product page.
- A machine readable licence: Publish a machine-readable licence for the product.
- Listed in a public inventory: Add the product to the public data inventory already published.
- A machine readable change history: Publish a version history for the product.

A check is pass where every one of an agency's data pages meets it, fail where none do, and partial where some do and some do not; a page that returned an access denial, an unconfirmable absence or a server error is counted as not meeting the check, and an agency with one data page can only pass or fail. The fix under a check is the action for the failing outcome the most agencies hit on that check across this measurement. Measured across all sixteen federal statistical agencies in October 2026.
